Clothes
KLōTHZ
n. pl. (rendering Hebrew beged and simlah, Greek himation and sparganon)
From Old English clath, cloth. The Hebrew beged is the general word for a garment, and it comes from a root meaning to act treacherously or cover over — the same consonants giving both garment and deal falsely, since a covering may conceal as well as clothe. Scripture exploits the ambiguity: clothes both dignify and disguise, and the rending of them is the standard sign that what was hidden has come out.

Biblical Definition

Clothes in Scripture mark the great transitions of a life, and they are placed at the two ends of the Lord's own. At the beginning: “And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luk 2:7) — the swaddling bands being the ordinary wrapping of any poor child, and the appointed sign given to the shepherds, so that the mark of the Messiah was that He looked like anyone else. At the other end, and at a graveside not His own: “And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go” (Joh 11:44) — Lazarus is raised but still bound, and the church is given the office of unbinding what Christ has made alive. The tearing of clothes is Scripture's standard sign of grief or of horror, and it is at the trial that the gesture becomes a self-condemnation: “Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses?” (Mat 26:65) — the law forbade the high priest to rend his garments, and in tearing them to condemn the true High Priest he ended his own office by the act. Joel warns against the gesture without the substance: rend your heart, and not your garments. Clothing is finally the Bible's picture of righteousness, from the coats of skins in Eden to the fine linen which is the righteousness of saints.

Webster 1828 Definition

Garments; the covering of the body; and in Scripture the swaddling clothes of the infant Christ, the graveclothes Lazarus was loosed from, the clothes rent in grief or in judgment, and the raiment which figures righteousness given or lacked.

CLOTHES, n. plural of cloth. 1. Garments for the human body; dress; vestments; vesture.

2. The covering of a bed; bed clothes.

3. In Hebrew, a garment; from a root which also signifies to cover over or deal treacherously, a covering serving to conceal as well as to clothe.

4. To rend the clothes, an ancient token of grief, indignation, or horror. Gen. 37; Matt. 26.

5. In Scripture, wrapped him in swaddling clothes. Luke 2. Bound hand and foot with graveclothes. John 11.

Key Scripture

Luke 2:7 — "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn."

John 11:44 — "And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go."

Matthew 26:65 — "Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses? behold, now ye have heard his blasphemy."

Isaiah 26:20 — "Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast."

Modern Corruption

Outward religious gesture is substituted for inward repentance, so that the rending of garments continues while the heart is untouched — the very exchange Joel names and the high priest performed at the trial of Christ.

expand to see more

Joel's command — rend your heart, and not your garments — identifies the oldest substitution in religion: the visible act standing in for the invisible change. The gesture is not condemned in itself; tearing the clothes was a genuine expression of grief, and Scripture records it of Jacob, David, Job, and Paul without rebuke. What is condemned is the gesture performed instead of repentance, and its modern forms are numerous and respectable: the public apology carefully worded to concede nothing, the emotional response at a meeting that changes no habit, the season of religious observance that leaves the besetting sin exactly where it was. God's stated preference is not for less feeling but for more reality: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.

Mat 26:65 is the most terrible instance in Scripture, and its detail rewards attention. The law expressly forbade the high priest to rend his clothes, on pain of death; in tearing them to pronounce the true High Priest a blasphemer, Caiaphas performed the outward sign of horror at blasphemy while committing it, and by the act publicly ended the office he was defending. The principle to recover is the one Lazarus's graveclothes illustrate from the other side (Joh 11:44): what Christ makes alive He also intends to be unbound, and the church's work with a raised man is to loose him and let him go — not to leave him in the wrappings of a life he has been brought out of. Religion that only tears cloth leaves the man exactly as he was; the gospel raises him and then takes the bandages off.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew beged is a garment, from a root meaning to cover over or deal treacherously; simlah is an outer wrapper or mantle. Greek himation is an outer garment, sparganon a swaddling band, and keiria the graveclothes of Lazarus.

expand to see more

Hebrew beged (H899) — a garment or covering; from bāgad, to cover over, and so to act treacherously, a covering that may conceal.

Hebrew simlah (H8071) — a mantle or outer wrapper; the garment taken in pledge which must be returned before sundown (Exo 22:26).

Hebrew qāra' b'gādīm — to rend the garments; the standard sign of mourning or horror, forbidden to the high priest (Lev 21:10).

Greek sparganon — a swaddling band; whence sparganoo, to wrap in swaddling clothes (Luk 2:7), the ordinary wrapping of an infant.

Greek keiria (G2750) — a winding sheet or bandage; bound hand and foot with graveclothes (Joh 11:44).

Usage

"Of the sign given to the shepherds: wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger (Luk 2:7)."

"Of the raised man still bound: bound hand and foot with graveclothes... Loose him, and let him go (Joh 11:44)."

"Of the gesture that condemned its maker: then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy (Mat 26:65)."
